findings.title: Password reset tokens are written to request logs
findings.evidence: A request to /api/auth/reset-password/AUDIT_RESET_TOKEN_NOT_SECRET returned 302 and emitted the complete token-bearing pathname in the incoming-request log. Better Auth generates real reset links using this path and leaves the token usable until reset or expiry.
findings.impact: A reader of application logs can obtain a live password reset credential, including for administrator accounts.
findings.remediation: Redact token-bearing path segments using route-aware logging for all auth surfaces. Apply equivalent rules to platform access logs where configurable.
findings.resolution: Request logging redacts reset-token path segments, including encoded routes, slashes and newlines; query strings remain omitted.

findings.title: Ordinary members can read complete farm contact and notes records
findings.evidence: A freshly invited customer received HTTP 200 from farms.list, including the fixture contactPhone and notes. The query selects every farm column and requires membership rather than administrator access.
findings.impact: All network members can retrieve farm operational notes and phone numbers through the direct backend even though the storefront browser proxy omits this procedure.
findings.remediation: Separate the minimal farm-selector projection from administrator farm records, or require administrator access for the complete list.

findings.title: Anonymous API requests can repeatedly cause unbudgeted database work
findings.impact: Successful inventory caching does not protect missing-network probes, invitation reads, readiness queries, or DB-backed CORS and network resolution. This provides avoidable DB load amplification; an outage was not load-tested.
findings.remediation: Apply a cheap request budget before DB access, cache network/CORS configuration, consider bounded negative caching, and restrict or briefly cache DB readiness checks. Add an explicit RPC batch-size limit.
findings.resolution: Before DB hooks, bounded per-client and per-process request budgets reject excess traffic with 429 and Retry-After. RPC batches are capped at ten operations. Concurrent CORS reads share a 30-second cache, readiness results a one-second cache, and missing inventory networks a five-second negative cache.

findings.title: Storefront auth loses client IP identity and can share rate-limit buckets
findings.evidence: Both storefront forwarding paths omit verified client-IP metadata. A production-mode local probe with no IP header placed reset requests in no-trusted-ip|/request-password-reset; five requests succeeded and the sixth returned 429.
findings.impact: Depending on the deployed proxy chain, users may share a fallback or frontend-egress-IP budget, allowing one user to exhaust authentication limits for others. Vercel overwrites forwarded IP headers, so the exact production bucket requires deployment verification.
findings.remediation: Carry authenticated, trusted client identity across proxy hops and configure Better Auth to use it. Never trust a raw client-supplied forwarding header.
findings.currentState: Proxy signing was removed at the user’s request. The API uses trusted platform or socket addresses; proxied visitors share the frontend server address for rate limits.
